title: Local certificate size versus verification radius
formal: Determine the worst-case certificate-size function \[F(s,d)=\max\{c_d(P):P\text{ is a graph property and }c_1(P)\le s\},\qquad s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1},\] in the anonymous local-verification model defined below. Here \(c_d(P)\) is the minimum number of certificate bits per vertex permitting sound and complete verification of \(P\) at radius \(d\), uniformly over all finite graphs. This asks for the whole numerical tradeoff, with pointwise absolute accuracy \(1/100\), rather than only a yes-or-no answer to the source’s proposed inverse-radius scaling.

source_formulation.text: Is it true that if we allow the verification algorithm to look at distance d, then the optimal size is at most \(\alpha  \cdot  s/d [\ldots ]\)
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 3

why: Local certificates let every vertex check a global claim using a small neighborhood. Understanding their dependence on verification radius would distinguish properties for which additional communication reliably reduces stored proof information from properties that retain an irreducible local memory cost.
status_note: The inverse-radius question is explicitly open in the 2024 source. This card documents a selected anonymous branch and a stronger full-function target. Checked later radius-reduction, certification-landscape and local-advice results do not determine it; later checks through 2026-09-16 are bounded.

progress.text: The STACS paper formulates the tradeoff conjecture, gives an exact anonymous radius-one bound for colorability, and proves radius tradeoffs for several specific properties.
The checked preprint on decreasing verification radius studies the reverse conversion and its dependence on degree, radius loss, certificate length and input size.
The DISC paper develops a complexity landscape on several graph classes. Its results do not identify the full function specified here.

category_assignment.reason: The resource tradeoff is explicitly for local distributed certificates and verification radius.

importance.reason: The tradeoff asks whether increased local visibility can universally replace stored proof information, even for graph properties with constant-size certificates. This probes a basic resource relationship in distributed verification and the memory needed for locally checkable evidence, beyond any single graph problem.
importance.basis: Individual reading of STACS 2024 Open problem 2 and its anonymous model, compared with later radius-reduction and certification-landscape results.

sentences: Local certification assigns a short proof string to every vertex so that a global graph property can be checked from nearby information.
The selected model has no identifiers or input labels, and certificate bounds must hold uniformly over all finite graphs.
For each initial bit budget and verification radius, the target is the largest minimum certificate size among properties certifiable within that budget at radius one.
The source asks whether certificate size always scales inversely with radius; this card explicitly asks for the full underlying worst-case function.
Determining the function would quantify when greater local visibility can replace stored proof information, with a Lean-certified error of at most one hundredth of a bit at every parameter pair.

definitions:
Graphs are finite, nonempty, simple and undirected; they may be disconnected and have arbitrary degree. A graph property \(P\) is a set of these graphs invariant under graph isomorphism. Vertices have no identifiers, port numbers, input labels, advice or knowledge of the graph order. Graph distance is the minimum number of edges in a path; vertices in different components have infinite distance.

Fix integers \(d\ge1\) and \(b\ge0\). A certificate assignment is any function \(z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\); for \(b=0\) there is one empty certificate. At a root \(v\), the radius-\(d\) view consists of the root, all vertices at distance at most \(d\), their certificates, and precisely the graph edges with at least one endpoint at distance at most \(d-1\) from \(v\). Edges between two vertices at distance exactly \(d\) are not visible. Neither edges leading beyond the view nor the degrees of its boundary vertices outside the view are additional input.

A verifier is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program accepting or rejecting a view. A view is encoded by its finite adjacency matrix, root index and certificate strings; the decision must be invariant under all renumberings of that encoding. Thus encoding indices convey no persistent identifiers. The program halts on every finite view. Its running time and memory are unrestricted, and it may depend on \(P,d,b\), but it is the same program for every graph order and every vertex. It has no oracle, random bits or additional input.

Such a verifier certifies \(P\) with \(b\) bits when, for every allowed graph \(G\),
\[
G\in P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\ \ \forall v\in V(G),\
A(\operatorname{view}_d(G,z,v))=\operatorname{accept}.
\]
The existential certificate assignment is unrestricted and may depend on the entire graph. On a graph outside \(P\), every assignment must cause at least one vertex to reject. There is no error probability. The cost is the common maximum number \(b\) of certificate bits stored at a vertex, not the total number of bits in the graph or view. Using a subset of the \(2^b\) strings is allowed.

Define \(c_d(P)\) as the least such integer \(b\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such verifier exists. The domain of the maximum in \(F(s,d)\) consists only of properties with a certificate bound \(s\) independent of graph order. Different properties and different values of \(d\) may use different verifiers; no algorithm receiving a description of \(P\) is required. The set of possible values is a nonempty subset of \(\{0,\ldots,s\}\): the property containing every graph has cost zero, and a radius-\(d\) verifier can restrict its input to radius one. Hence this maximum is finite and attained as a numerical value. All graphs, graph orders, properties and degrees in its definition are quantified; neither \(s\) nor \(d\) is hidden in an unspecified constant.
answer_criterion: Supply a mathematically specified function \(g:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(\lvert g(s,d)-F(s,d)\rvert\le1/100\) for every \(s\ge0,d\ge1\). The approximation need not be integer-valued. An unambiguous expression or certified rule can specify \(g\); merely repeating the defining maximum, giving sampled values, or proving only asymptotic upper or lower bounds does not determine this function to the required precision.

context_blocks.text: Open problem 2 asks whether allowing distance \(d\) reduces optimal certificate size \(s\) to at most a constant times \(s/d\), including dependence on the parameters of local properties. It does not specify all rounding and uniformity conventions for a numerical benchmark.

This card explicitly selects the source’s anonymous model and the branch of unlabeled graph properties admitting a constant certificate bound for all graph orders. It broadens the threshold question to the underlying worst-case function \(F(s,d)\), following the authorized quantity/function review. Determining this function is a stronger quantitative target, not an assertion that it is equivalent to every version of the source conjecture. Identifier-dependent models, properties with separate vertex inputs and bounds growing with graph order are outside this selected branch.

The radius view follows Definition 15, including the omission of edges between outer-boundary vertices. A finite terminating verification program fixes computational uniformity, while local running time is unrestricted.

The source proves that anonymous radius-one certification of \(k\)-colorability requires exactly \(\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\) bits. Its larger-radius lower bound and upper bounds for selected properties illustrate the tradeoff, without establishing a universal compression theorem.

The later paper on decreasing verification radius studies how certificate sizes grow when a verifier must see less. Its bounds for that direction do not determine the cost of increasing the radius in the model of this card.

The 2025 complexity-landscape paper studies possible certificate growth rates on paths, cycles and trees, with distinctions involving identifiers and knowledge of graph order. These are different from the full worst-case function for constant certificate bounds on arbitrary graphs.

Checked arXiv:2312.13702v2, 26 December 2023, against the published formulation. The publisher date does not imply a later revised proof.

Read the radius-reduction preprint arXiv:2408.10757v1, 20 August 2024, Sections 1.1–1.2 and conclusion, and verified the 2025 journal citation on the author page. Its identifier-based radius-decrease transformation is not a universal inverse tradeoff.
Read DISC 2025 Article 18 Introduction and Sections 1.1–1.3 for the scope of its graph-class and certificate-growth results, without claiming full proof verification.

Checked the primary DISC 2025 local-advice publication and Section 1.8: it concerns distributed computation with advice and leaves related coloring questions open. This is not a certification theorem for the function defined here.

Model check: restriction to radius one gives c_d(P)<=c_1(P), so the defining set of values for F is nonempty and bounded by s. Quantification across properties makes the resource function uniform in parameters rather than allowing a scaling constant to hide the initial certificate size.

Bounded subsequent searches and author-publication checks through 2026-09-16 verified no complete solution of this selected tradeoff function. No exhaustive present-open certification or Lean formalization is claimed.
